clinicalPearls: Congenital, localised absence of skin most often affecting the vertex of the scalp, presenting at birth as a well-demarcated ulcer, membranous defect or already-healed atrophic scar.
The majority are solitary midline scalp lesions; larger or multiple defects and those overlying the spine or trunk warrant a search for associated anomalies.
The membranous variant is often surrounded by a collar of long, dark hair (the hair collar sign), which is a marker of possible underlying neural tube or cranial dysraphism.
A visible pulsation or bluish translucency at the base suggests an underlying bony defect with exposed dura or a sagittal sinus, raising the risk of haemorrhage and meningitis.
Adams-Oliver syndrome links scalp aplasia cutis with terminal transverse limb reduction defects and cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita; screen for these when a scalp defect is found.
Truncal or limb defects in a stillborn or macerated co-twin distribution suggest the fetus papyraceus association from intrauterine death of a monozygotic twin.
Small defects heal spontaneously by secondary intention with conservative wound care, leaving a hairless atrophic scar; large defects may need surgical closure or grafting.
Bart syndrome describes aplasia cutis of the lower limbs in association with epidermolysis bullosa, so blistering elsewhere should prompt investigation for inherited EB.
reference.pathophysiology: Aplasia cutis congenita is a heterogeneous developmental defect in which localised interruption of skin formation leaves epidermis, dermis and occasionally deeper structures absent at birth. It is not a single disease but a phenotype with multiple mechanisms, including intrauterine vascular compromise, thrombotic or embolic events (as with a demised co-twin), amniotic membrane adherence, teratogen exposure such as methimazole, and single-gene disorders affecting skin or vascular development. Failure of closure of embryonic fusion lines may explain midline scalp predilection, while defective proliferation or premature degeneration of skin at biomechanical tension points may account for lesions over rapidly growing areas. When the defect extends through the skull, meninges or dura may be exposed, and the underlying dural sinuses are vulnerable to injury.
additionalDifferentials: obstetric scalp trauma from forceps, vacuum or fetal scalp electrode
birth-related caput succedaneum or cephalohaematoma with overlying breakdown
epidermolysis bullosa with congenital localised skin absence
naevus sebaceus of Jadassohn on the scalp
encephalocoele or meningocoele with cutaneous defect
herpes simplex or bacterial neonatal skin ulceration
additionalInvestigations: cranial ultrasound or MRI when a bony defect, hair collar sign or midline lesion suggests dysraphism
plain skull radiography or CT to delineate underlying calvarial defects
dermatological and skeletal examination for limb reduction defects (Adams-Oliver)
echocardiography and vascular assessment where a syndromic association is suspected
karyotype or targeted genetic testing when multiple anomalies coexist
skin biopsy of atypical lesions to exclude epidermolysis bullosa or naevus sebaceus
placental and co-twin examination for evidence of fetus papyraceus
redFlags: visible dural or sagittal sinus pulsation, or bluish translucency indicating exposed intracranial contents and haemorrhage risk
large or deep defect with exposed bone or brain, carrying risk of meningitis and life-threatening bleeding
hair collar sign or midline location suggesting underlying neural tube defect
signs of local infection with purulence, surrounding cellulitis or systemic sepsis
associated limb, cardiac or gastrointestinal anomalies indicating a syndromic diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Small solitary scalp defects have an excellent prognosis, healing spontaneously with a residual atrophic hairless scar. Large defects, exposed dura or associated syndromic anomalies carry higher morbidity, with risk of haemorrhage, infection and dependence on surgical reconstruction.
pitfalls: attributing a scalp defect to birth trauma and missing a true congenital lesion or its syndromic associations
overlooking the hair collar sign and failing to image for underlying dysraphism
aggressively debriding or grafting a small membranous lesion that would heal conservatively
not examining the limbs, heart and skin elsewhere for Adams-Oliver, Bart or Goltz features
underestimating haemorrhage risk in lesions overlying the sagittal sinus
